title: Dagesh, Meteg, and Reading Checkpoint
description: Distinguish dagesh lene and forte, and consolidate reading.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: A dot inside a letter is a dagesh. It has two unrelated jobs. Dagesh lene appears in the six letters ב ג ד כ פ ת (begadkefat) and hardens the sound — bet from v to b, pe from f to p, and so on. Dagesh forte doubles the consonant, holding a vowel before it and strengthening the letter. Telling them apart comes from the letters and the preceding vowel, and doing so is part of accurate reading.

blocks.caption: Dagesh
rows: hardens b, g, d, k, p, t

blocks.caption: Dagesh lene
blocks.html: The six begadkefat letters have two pronunciations, a hard (stopped) and a soft (spirant) one. After a vowel they usually soften; at the start of a word, after a consonant, or after a silent shewa they harden, and that hardening is marked by dagesh lene. So ב can be b (with dagesh) or v (without), and כ can be k or kh.

blocks.caption: Dagesh forte
blocks.html: Dagesh forte doubles the consonant: שַׁבָּת (šabbāt) has a doubled bet. It normally follows a vowel, which the doubling closes off, and it appears in any letter, not only the six. It often marks a grammatical doubling, as when a root letter is strengthened.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: A dot in a begadkefat letter might be lene or forte; the distinction is that lene never follows a vowel, while forte usually does. Read the word, check what precedes the dot, and let the syllable decide. Meteg, a small vertical stroke beside a vowel, is a different mark that only guides reading; it does not change sound.
